title: Arguments with Types That Express Their Purpose

blocks.text: Two Integers Can Have Different Roles

A seat reservation needs a total capacity and a current occupancy. If both arguments were int, swapping them would produce a call with correct types. Parameter names help us read a declaration, but they do not let the compiler distinguish the roles of two integers at a call site. We can express each role with a user-defined type.

Capacidad and Ocupacion will be structs with a member named unidades. Capacidad and Ocupacion are different types even though both contain an int. First we use the types to prevent mixing up roles; then the constructor checks the numerical rules.

blocks.question: Which error do these two distinct types help detect?
options: Requesting an occupancy greater than the capacity.
Supplying a value outside the allowed domain inside Capacidad.
Swapping capacity and occupancy in a call.
blocks.explanation: The other two errors still provide values of the expected type and require validation of the rules.

blocks.text: Construct Arguments with Their Roles Visible

Capacidad{8} constructs an argument that names its role; Ocupacion{3} does the same for occupied seats. The constructor's initializer list reads the unidades member of each parameter and initializes its own members. Validation requires capacity from one to twenty and occupancy from zero through capacity.

blocks.text: Mixing Roles Is a Type Error

blocks.question: Why is this call rejected before execution?
options: The number two is always an invalid occupancy.
Ocupacion does not match the first parameter, which expects Capacidad.
The constructor automatically swaps the two arguments.
blocks.explanation: The problem is the argument type, even though the numbers could form a valid reservation in the correct order.

blocks.text: We do not add automatic conversions between these structs or from a bare int. Keeping the role of each argument visible preserves the distinction we just introduced.

blocks.text: An Interface Sufficient for Derived Queries

Capacity can never be zero in a correctly constructed object. That rule justifies the division. The literal 100.0 makes the calculation use double. The function receives a const reference and uses public queries: it does not need to write to the private representation. The usual output may round the approximation; no fixed decimal format is specified here.
Transfer the Distinction Between Argument Roles

Design Caja with the types Ancho and Alto, each containing an int member called unidades. Caja keeps its dimensions in private members. Its constructor takes Ancho first and then Alto; both values must be between one and ten. Reject other values with CajaInvalida. Provide const queries ancho(), alto(), and area(). Construct a width of three and a height of four, displaying 3:4:12. Test one and ten in each dimension, as well as neighboring values zero and eleven. Also check that swapping the argument types causes a compilation diagnostic; remove that call before running the valid tests.

The area fits in int for this domain: its maximum is one hundred. Justify that limit before multiplying. Distinct types prevent swapping dimensions, while numerical validation serves a different purpose.
Reference Solution and Criteria for Argument Roles

Criteria: the parameter types reflect the order of the roles; all four valid endpoints are preserved; zero and eleven are rejected for either dimension; members are private; queries work on const objects; and area is calculated from the actual dimensions. The constructor body does not have to match this implementation exactly.
